Added in session 72 (headphone 3D's timbre, §3.1 #47; `code/macos/macos_snd.c`, folded into 9f's commit d96b9381; §2 "Session 72"):
- **The EQ:** the spatial mixer's output goes through a gain and three biquads, the same on both ears (the interaural cues untouched): +1.01 dB (`SND_SPATIAL_DB`), a high shelf at 659 Hz −1.15 dB (Q 0.67), peaks at 7393 Hz −2.57 dB (Q 3.72) and 12672 Hz −4.25 dB (Q 1.90) (`snd_spatialEQ`). Fitted (`build.noindex/s72/probes/fit.py`) to the inverse of Apple's HRTF's mean timbre over the horizon (every azimuth, elevations −30 to 30; both ears' power against the stereo pans' ahead, power 1 at every side, since the HRTF has its own front and back; 40 Hz–15 kHz, smoothed to a third of an octave; no boost above 15 kHz), 0.30 dB rms residual. It replaces `SND_SPATIAL_GAIN`. A sound ahead keeps Apple's frontal brightness in part (+1.3 dB at 2.5–5 kHz, +2.5 at 12.5–16 against stereo); the front's EQ (a sound ahead exactly stereo's) was the alternative, which the user didn't hear apart.
- **In the render:** RBJ's cookbook biquads computed in double at the mix rate in `SND_SpatialInit` (so again at a new device rate, the IO thread stopped), the gain in the first stage's numerator; a stage at 0.45 of the rate or above passes (a Bluetooth headset's 16 or 24 kHz: the 12.7 and 7.4 kHz stages). `SND_SpatialEQ` runs each ear of the unit's block through the cascade (transposed direct form II, float) into the mix, before the master gain and the limiter; its state is cleared when the unit stops rendering (no input enabled), so a sound from rest renders the same every time. Cost +0.33 to +0.48 µs per ms of audio while headphone 3D renders, nothing in stereo (the unit isn't made); no buffering, no added latency.

Added in session 75 (§3.1 #49; `code/macos/macos_window.m`, `code/renderer_metal/tr_mtl.m`; built and checked offline, not run in the game: the monitors were off):
- **`r_blackOutDisplays 1`** (archived, not latched: the next frame applies it; default 0): a `MacOSCoverWindow` per other display (`MTLimp_GetDisplays`' list: no mirrors), borderless, opaque black, no shadow, drawn once (no content but its background), `canBecomeKeyWindow` and `canBecomeMainWindow` NO, `ignoresMouseEvents` YES, at `CGShieldingWindowLevel()`, `CanJoinAllSpaces | Stationary | IgnoresCycle | FullScreenAuxiliary | FullScreenDisallowsTiling | CanJoinAllApplications`, out of the Windows menu, no ordering animation. Up (`MTLimp_UpdateCovers`) while `MTLimp_WantCovers`: the cvar on, the game window key and not minimized, no `Sys_Dialog` up, and exclusive up (`mac_exclusiveActive`), or the borderless window (`MAC_DESKTOPWINDOW`), or the Space once entered and only when `NSScreen.screensHaveSeparateSpaces`. Updated at the window's key, resign, miniaturize and deminiaturize, the Space's enter and exit (down already at its *will* exit), exclusive's enter, a display change (`NSApplicationDidChangeScreenParametersNotification`, the game's own mode switch included) and the cvar's change (`MTLimp_EndFrame`); down first thing in `MTLimp_LeaveExclusive` (a focus loss, Cmd+Tab with the displays captured, a dialog) and in `MacOS_DialogBegin` in every mode; destroyed in `MTLimp_DestroyWindow` (vid_restart, quit). The frames come from `CGDisplayBounds` (`MTLimp_DisplayFrame`: current right after a mode switch). One log line when the number of covered displays changes, and one when the Space leaves the blanking to macOS (the displays share their Spaces).
  - *Why each choice:* **the level** is exclusive's own, because a mode switch on the main display captures every display (`CGCaptureAllDisplays`, as SDL did) and a captured display shows only windows at the shielding level or above; it also covers what animates above normal windows on the other display (its own menu bar with separate Spaces, the Dock, notification banners). Whatever needs the player takes the keyboard, which takes the covers down. **Clicks pass through:** while the game has the mouse the cursor is detached from it and parked at the game window's center (`IN_Capture`), so it never reaches a covered display and the capture needs nothing new; a free cursor (`in_mouse 0`, the only case in fullscreen) clicks what it would click without the cover instead of a black window swallowing it. **The borderless window too:** session 26 measured the same loss there (11.8–13.8% of frames shown by a later one; covered 0.1%). **The Space only with separate Spaces:** without them macOS blanks the other displays itself (sessions 23 and 26: the 4K never swapped). **Never a plain window:** there the other displays are what the player wants to see. **Why the covers probably work** (from session 39, not proven): capturing the displays left 22% of the frames replaced although a capture blanks them, while a still window over the 4K brought it to 0.8%; so the cost isn't the 4K being composited but the covered applications' own frames, which they stop drawing once their windows are occluded (Chromium, WebKit and AppKit throttle on occlusion). An application that draws regardless would still cost frames; `measure75.sh`'s `BUSY=gpu20` tells.
  - *At 0:* every new call returns before any WindowServer call while no cover exists (`MTLimp_WantCovers` false, `MTLimp_HideCovers` over none); the new delegate methods and the observer only make that call, and nothing is logged.
- *`r_metalPacedPresent` was removed in session 79 (61e24ec2 reverts 01092821) once the covers were measured with both monitors on (§2 "Session 79", §3.1 #54); the design below is the record, should a visible other display ever need it.* **`r_metalPacedPresent`** (archived, latched; default 0), an experiment: with **1** the frames never present; a `CAMetalDisplayLink` on its own thread ("openmohaa presents", user-interactive QoS, its own run loop, stopped through a run-loop source) asks once per refresh of the game's display for that refresh's drawable (`preferredFrameLatency` 1, the rate the display's), and the newest frame committed by then goes into it (`MBPacer`). The layer is synced to the display (`displaySyncEnabled YES`, whatever `r_swapInterval` says) with 3 drawables (`r_metalDrawables` 0). With **2** the frame is taken `r_metalPacedMargin` µs (not archived, read live, default 1000, clamped 0–8000) before the link's deadline (`targetTimestamp`) instead of when the link asks.
  - *The survey:* **`presentDrawable:atTime:` / `presentDrawable:afterMinimumDuration:`** time each frame's present, but every frame still presents: at 480 on 240 Hz two presents a refresh, which queue with vsync (each present takes a refresh: with 2 drawables fullscreen showed each frame 11.9 ms after it, §2's session 5, and ran at half the refresh rate, the layer's comment in `macos_window.m`) or tear without it (exclusive now); the display's refresh times would be ours to find too. **§4b part 4's display sync with a just-in-time frame start** moves the frame's start (the engine's limiter) to the refresh: that changes frame pacing and with it the stock mode's usercmds, which CLAUDE.md rules out without the user, and #37 dropped it. **`CAMetalDisplayLink`** (macOS 14+) hands out one drawable per refresh with its deadline and presentation time from the system, which knows the WindowServer's latching; Apple's documentation: `preferredFrameLatency` takes only 1.0 or 2.0 ("the final latency may be bigger if the system needs more time, such as for windowed modes on macOS"), the frame rate range defaults to the display's maximum, and `targetTimestamp` is "a deadline that indicates when your app needs to finish rendering to the drawable". **Chosen: the link drives only the presents**, the engine's loop stays as it is, and the mailbox (the newest frame per refresh, the older ones replaced) is ours.
  - *The protocol:* the frame's command buffer has no final pass; `MB_CommitPaced` commits it under `mb_pacedLock` and leaves the frame's number, gamma ramp and cl_latencyStats record there; the link's handler takes the newest under the same lock (nothing new: no present, the screen keeps its frame) and `enqueue`s its command buffer there, then outside the lock encodes the final pass from the one scene texture into the link's drawable, presents and commits. The queue's order and Metal's hazard tracking of the scene texture make that final pass read exactly the frame it took: it runs after that frame and before the next one's scene pass. A frame that commits part of its scene (`MB_FlushAndWait`, a readback) sets a hold under the lock first, and no present takes the scene until that frame ends. A frame no present took before the next one commits is replaced: its record says not presented (the probe then gives its input to the next frame shown). `mbShutdown` stops the link before it commits anything. `r_metalPresentStats` reports the link's updates, the presents, the updates with nothing new or held, those past their deadline, the frames replaced, and the mean (deadline − call) and (presentation − deadline).
  - *What it keeps and costs:* the engine's loop runs as with vsync off: no frame waits for a drawable or a refresh (no `nextDrawable` on the main thread, no late presents, the frames-in-flight wait as before), so `com_maxfps`, the stock mode's usercmds and the decoupled mode's clock are unchanged; the final pass runs once per refresh instead of once per frame (at 480 on 240 Hz half as often). The latency: the frame shown was committed before the link's call, about a refresh ahead of its presentation (1), or `r_metalPacedMargin` before the deadline (2): against vsync off up to about a refresh more (~4.2 ms at 240 Hz), to be measured; paced presents never tear.
  - *Why 3 drawables:* one present per refresh queues nothing, so the third adds no latency as it does with vsync off (session 26); it is there because the link asks for the coming refresh's drawable while the one on screen and the one presented for this refresh may both still be held (with 2 the link would wait for one to come back, ~0.25–0.33 ms after a flip, or miss its refresh). `r_metalDrawables 2` tries 2.
  - *Checked offline* (`build.noindex/s75/pacedcheck.m`, headless Metal on the M4, no display): the same lock, state and order of calls, the drawable replaced by a one-pixel readback of the scene; the frames as fast as the GPU goes, then at 480 a second, each a 64 MB blit and a clear to its number, one in seven with a half-done scene first behind the hold; the "link" at 240 Hz with a jitter. 677 presents of 5143 frames (4466 replaced; 761 updates held): **every present read exactly the frame it took, none a half-done scene, every record ended exactly once**. The negative control (`PACEDCHECK_BROKEN=1`: the enqueue after the lock) fails: 255 wrong pixels, 47 half-done scenes, so the check sees the race.
  - *At 0:* `mb_paced` is 0, so the layer's drawable count and display sync, the drawable thread, late presents, the frame's commit and the log line are the same expressions as before; the hold and the shutdown's stop are skipped.

Added in session 78 (§3.1 #52; `code/renderer_metal/tr_backend.c`, `tr_shade.c`, `tr_shader.c`, `tr_init.c`, `tr_local.h`, `tr_mtl.h`, `tr_mtl.m`; `code/client/cl_input.cpp`; `code/fgame/player.cpp`, `code/cgame/cg_predict.c`):
- **`r_depthClamp`, the Metal way:** depth clamp is the render encoder's depth clip mode (`setDepthClipMode:`), not pipeline state as on Vulkan, so no pipeline variants and no precache change. The front end asks for it per batch: `RB_EndSurface` enables the GL-style cap `MB_DEPTH_CLAMP` around the shader's iterator when `RB_DepthClampBatch` says so (the shader's class, `shader_t.depthClamp`, set once in `FinishShader`: solid for sorts SS_OPAQUE–SS_BANNER and for blended sorts SS_UNDERWATER–SS_BLEND6 with a depth-writing stage, translucent for the rest of those, none for the sky, portals and later sorts; then the world entity always, static models and entities at 2: solid, or any static model's; never sprite batches, 2D, or views without the world), so every pass of a surface has the same setting and the depth-equal passes match. `MB_PrepareDraw` sets the encoder's mode only when the effective state changes (`mb_encDepthClamp`, reset with each new encoder, whose default clips), and only with the full depth range [0, 1]: the view weapon's [0, 0.3] and the debug views' ranges clip. **The floor:** with `r_depthClamp` on, `RB_BeginDrawingView` sets `mbDepthFloor(0.3)` and a requested full range [0, 1] becomes the viewport's [0.3, 1], so a wall clamped at the near plane (depth 0.3) never hides the weapon (≤ 0.3); `mbDepthQuery` maps its point's depth the same way (the flares); the clear quads keep [0, 1] (a clear value is absolute). Off (`r_depthClamp 0`): the floor is 0 and no cap is ever set: one test per batch and two per draw, the same encoder calls as before.
- **`cl_nullbinds`:** `CL_PairKey` wraps `IN_KeyDown`/`IN_KeyUp` for the three pairs (forward/back, the strafes, the leans by name and as `button4`/`button5`). A press with the cvar on makes the other side inactive with JayRewd's credit (since 63a44882, after the user's "use his math"; f127395d used IN_KeyUp's): its time from `downtime` to the press, nothing when the press is stamped before `downtime` (the input stamps a key with the previous input read's time, up to about 1 ms before the step began), half a frame without a time stamp; and drops its tap (`wasPressed`); a full release of a side left inactive keeps the credit it had (IN_KeyUp's would count again from its stale `downtime`); the winner's full release makes a side still held active from the release's time (`downtime`), and drops the winner's tap. Releases do this with the cvar at 0 too, so a side left out while it was on comes back; at 0 a held side is always active, so nothing of this runs.
Added in session 79 (§3.1 #54; `code/macos/macos_window.m`; built, not run in the game: the 4K was off and the user remote). *`r_metalComposited` was removed the same day (c217f900 reverts 5b055f83; the user: "Yes, remove it"); the design below is the record, should GL1's composited way be wanted again:*
- **`r_metalComposited 1`** (archived, latched; default 0), an experiment: every fullscreen mode's window keeps its shadow (`hasShadow YES`, the borderless and the Space's windows alike), and the shadow's offscreen pass keeps the layer from going direct to display (session 6, Instruments: "layer requires a potential offscreen render"), so the WindowServer composites the game into the display as it composited GL1's fullscreen (§2's session 5: GL1's fullscreen surface was never direct). One log line when on ("r_metalComposited: through the compositor, not direct to display"). Meant with **`r_metalPacedPresent 1`**: one present per refresh into a synced layer, which the compositor shows at its refresh: GL1's way of showing frames (whole, the newest each refresh), at about one more refresh than paced presents alone (~4 ms at 240 Hz; to be measured). Alone, with vsync off, it is what a window does (session 6: the compositor then swaps at the game's present rate, session 5 at the display's: its two modes).
  - *Why the shadow:* it is the cause session 6 measured and removed; a window over the whole screen casts it outside the screen, so nothing shows. The fallback if a trace shows the layer still direct: `mac_layer.opaque = NO`, the other documented condition (the final pass writes alpha 1, `tr_mtl_final.metal`, so the picture would be the same).
  - *Why it might not help:* the compositor is the same WindowServer that holds the direct flips; no run has composited fullscreen with the 4K busy (session 39's composited window at 250, the Claude app on the 4K: pump → present p95 4.3–4.5 ms, as exclusive's 3.9, every frame shown by its own frame). `measure75.sh`'s `comp` block measures it.
  - *At 0:* `hasShadow` is set NO for every fullscreen window, the same assignment as before, and nothing is logged; windowed mode is untouched either way.
- **`build.noindex/s75/measure75.sh`'s session 79 blocks**, each A B B A against exclusive as it is: `cap240` (`com_maxfps 240`), `vsync` (`r_swapInterval 1`) (`comp` and `compoff`, `r_metalComposited` with and without paced presents, went with the cvar); the common arguments now come before the variant's, so a variant overrides `com_maxfps` and `r_swapInterval` (no earlier variant sets what they set: their runs are unchanged). `sum75.py` prints each display's direct-to-display counts, the not-direct reasons (and would print an `r_metalComposited` line); checked on a synthetic run. The originals beside them as `.s75`.

## 4. Architecture of renderer_metal

```
client (cl_main, cgame, uilib)  --refexport_t/refimport_t (unchanged ABI)-->  renderer_metal
  front end (copied from GL1): BSP/world, shaders, images (CPU decode), TIKI/skeletor glue, terrain,
  marks, sky portal, fonts, tess/svars stage computation
        |  tr_mtl.h: GL-free C backend API (state bits, binds, draws, uploads, readback)
  backend (Objective-C, ARC): device/queue, frame ring, encoders, PSO/depth-stencil/sampler caches,
  textures, ring buffers, final pass, screenshots
        |
  sdl/sdl_mtlimp.m: SDL window (SDL_WINDOW_METAL | ALLOW_HIGHDPI) + SDL_Metal_CreateView -> CAMetalLayer
```

**Window layer (`sdl/sdl_mtlimp.m`, compiled into the renderer like sdl_glimp.c):**
- Same mode/fullscreen logic as `sdl_glimp.c` (`r_mode`, `r_customwidth/height`, `r_fullscreen`, `r_noborder`, desktop mode `-2`, live fullscreen toggle, resize → `vid_restart`). Calls `ri.IN_Init(window)`.
- `CAMetalLayer`: `BGRA8Unorm` (not sRGB: Q3 math is gamma-space), `framebufferOnly YES`, opaque, `maximumDrawableCount` 2, or 3 for vsync in fullscreen (`r_metalDrawables`, session 6), `displaySyncEnabled = r_swapInterval`, `presentsWithTransaction NO`, `drawableSize` = window pixels.
- HiDPI: drawable size in pixels → `glConfig.vidWidth/vidHeight`. Check the HUD/UI scaling on the 4K@2× display.
- Fills `glConfig` (renderer string "Apple M4 (Metal)", maxTextureSize 16384, stencil 8, no hardware gamma: gamma is applied in-shader).

**Frame model:**
- One `MTLCommandQueue`. 2 frames in flight by default (`r_metalFramesInFlight`; an `MTLSharedEvent` signaled by the GPU per frame, waited on right after commit). One command buffer per frame (`commandBufferWithUnretainedReferences`), begun lazily at the first draw or clear (2D exports draw outside the queue), plus an upload command buffer committed before it when textures in use are rewritten. Drawables: see §3.2 "Drawable acquisition".
- Rendering goes to an offscreen color target (`RGBA8Unorm`, private) + `Depth32Float_Stencil8`. At end of frame one fullscreen triangle copies it to the drawable and applies **gamma + overbright in the shader**, reproducing GL1's behavior per mode (overbright only where GL1 has it: fullscreen with hw gamma). Then present + commit. Never wait on the GPU except at shutdown and readback.
- Screenshots and video frames: blit from the offscreen target (pre-gamma, as GL1's back-buffer read) into a shared buffer, written out in the completion handler (async, no stall).

**Pipelines and shaders (`renderer_metal/shaders/*.metal`):**
- One generic stage shader pair (`shaders/tr_mtl_stage.metal`, session 3): function constants for the sampled texture units and alpha test on/off only; texenv per unit (modulate/replace/decal/add/combine), vertex vs constant color, the alpha function and reference, linear fog and the clip plane (`[[clip_distance]]`) are uniforms. Vertices fetched by hand from the frame ring (see §3.2 "Added in session 3").
- Separate small shaders: final pass (gamma/overbright), partial clears.
- PSO cache keyed by blend factors, RGB write mask, texture units and alpha test (formats are fixed). Depth/stencil state cache keyed by depth func/test/write + stencil func/ops/masks. Sampler cache by filter/mip/wrap/aniso/max LOD. `MTLBinaryArchive` on disk in `fs_homepath` (Phase 3/5).
- GL conventions in the backend: the front end keeps GL projection matrices; the backend remaps clip z from [-1,1] to [0,1] and flips the viewport/scissor origin (bottom-left → top-left). Front-face winding matches GL CCW after the flip. `glDepthRange` (weapon depth hack) → `MTLViewport` znear/zfar. Polygon offset → `setDepthBias`. GL lines → Metal line primitives.

**Resources:**
- Per-frame shared `MTLBuffer` ring (Apple Silicon unified memory) for tess vertices/indices (memcpy + `setVertexBuffer:offset:`). Small uniforms via `setVertexBytes`/`setFragmentBytes`.
- Textures: `image_t.texnum` → index into a backend texture table; handles are never reused while frames are in flight. RGBA8 uploads (CPU mips kept first for parity). DDS → BC1/BC3 (natively supported). Mid-frame re-uploads (cinematics, ghost textures, dlight lightmaps) use a small per-frame ring so recorded draws keep their contents. Deferred destruction after the frame's completion.
- Flares: replace the `glReadPixels` depth test with visibility-result (occlusion) queries or a depth read one frame late.

**Threading:** single-threaded, like GL1 (Metal encoding is cheap, and there's no driver thread to fight). A render thread or parallel encoding only if Phase 5 profiling shows the CPU is the limit. A render thread would add a frame of latency, so it needs a clear win to justify it (see §4b).

## 4b. Lowest input latency and overhead (user requirement, 2026-10-16)

The user's words: "can we also optimize for lowest input lag/delay possible? like lowest overhead". This sits alongside the Goal: every design choice is judged on input-to-photon latency and overhead as well as fps. The user plays competitively online on a 240 Hz display, currently in a 1920×1080 *window* on a 1920×1080 screen.

**The latency chain and what we control:**
mouse HID → macOS → SDL event pump (`IN_Frame`, once per frame) → `CL_SendCmd` builds the usercmd/view angles → cgame + renderer build the frame → GPU → present → WindowServer compositor (windowed) or direct-to-display (fullscreen) → scanout.
- The engine's frame order is already latency-friendly: Com_Frame sleeps in its frame limiter **before** pumping input, then samples input, then renders (`qcommon/common.c` Com_Frame → `client/cl_main.cpp:2830` `CL_SendCmd` → `:2852` `SCR_UpdateScreen`). Keep it that way: **no waiting between input sampling and rendering**.
- GL1 today: `glFinish` every frame (`tr_backend.c:1429`) plus a composited window (at least one extra refresh, ~4.2 ms at 240 Hz).

**Design rules (all phases):**
1. **Never block between input sampling and encoding.** Any wait for the GPU (frames-in-flight semaphore) or for a drawable happens at the *end* of the previous frame or right before the limiter sleep, never after `CL_SendCmd`. Acquire the drawable as late as possible (only for the final pass); present right after commit; `presentsWithTransaction NO`.
2. **Minimal queueing.** Frames in flight is a cvar (`r_metalFramesInFlight`, 1–3), and `CAMetalLayer.maximumDrawableCount` is 2 by default (3 only if measured to help). With ~0.2 ms of GPU work per frame, 1–2 frames in flight cost almost no throughput; pick the default by measuring latency *and* work time.
3. **`r_swapInterval 0` = immediate present** (`displaySyncEnabled NO`, tearing allowed in fullscreen) for the lowest latency. `1` = vsync, optionally paced with `CAMetalDisplayLink` (`preferredFrameLatency` 1) instead of blocking in `nextDrawable`.
4. **Fullscreen must hit direct-to-display** (compositor bypass): opaque layer, drawable size = native display pixels, no overlays or transforms. Verify with the Metal Performance HUD ("Direct") and Metal System Trace. Offer a borderless-fullscreen mode that keeps direct-to-display, so the user doesn't pay compositor latency for "windowed fullscreen". Tell the user that a plain window is always composited (+1 refresh). *Session 6: and no window shadow (a shadow forces an offscreen pass); measured with `display_trace.py`, which prints Instruments' reason when a frame isn't direct.*
5. **Game Mode and scheduling.** Info.plist `LSApplicationCategoryType = public.app-category.games` + `GCSupportsGameMode` (macOS Game Mode in fullscreen: CPU/GPU priority, doubled Bluetooth sampling for controllers and AirPods). While in a game: `NSProcessInfo beginActivityWithOptions: NSActivityLatencyCritical | NSActivityUserInitiated` (no App Nap, minimal timer coalescing), and the main thread at `QOS_CLASS_USER_INTERACTIVE` (P-cores). *Game Mode measured on against off in session 64 (§2 "Session 64"): the same latency and mean frame work, the bench's p95–p99 frame work higher with it on; the declaration stays until the user decides.*
6. **Low overhead in the hot path:** no per-frame heap allocations in the renderer or backend; one `@autoreleasepool` per frame; cached PSOs, depth/stencil and sampler states (no lookups by string); state changes filtered on the CPU; hidden visibility, LTO, and the renderer linked statically in Phase 4; no Objective-C in the front end; no GPU→CPU readbacks in the frame (flares/screenshots are async).
7. **Gameplay feel is not ours to change silently.** Anything that alters frame pacing or usercmd timing (the 1 ms frame floor, `com_maxfps` precision, `Sys_Milliseconds` resolution) affects movement and online feel: measure, propose, and get the user's OK first. The facts players rely on, which must stay exact:
   - The engine clock is whole milliseconds. `Com_Frame` uses `minMsec = 1000 / com_maxfps` (integer division, rounds down), and `bias` only catches up after a frame overran. So every value runs at even whole-ms frames, but values that don't divide 1000 are silently rounded *up* to the next rate that does: 240 → 4 ms frames = 250 fps, 144 → 6 ms = ~167 fps, 120 → 8 ms = 125 fps. Vanilla already wakes ~1 ms early and polls `select(0)` until the ms tick flips, so divisor rates are close to tick-exact today. The cost is ~1 ms of polling CPU per frame.
   - `com_maxfps` ≥ 1001 gives `minMsec 0`: no floor, and 0 ms frames are bumped to 1 ms by `Com_ModifyMsec` (`common.c:2188`), so the game clock runs fast (existing upstream bug). `com_maxfps 0` and timedemo use the 1 ms floor.
   - `cl_maxpackets` (clamped 30–125, default 30) sends a packet only when ≥ `1000 / cl_maxpackets` ms have passed since the last one (`client/cl_input.cpp:895-906`). Commands in between are bundled into the next packet, so none are lost. The real packet rate is fps / n: 250 fps + 125 packets = every 2nd frame (even, 125/s); 125 fps + 100 = every 2nd frame, only 62.5/s.
   - The server runs each usercmd as soon as its packet arrives (`server/sv_client.c:1963`); `sv_fps` is 20. There is no lag compensation anywhere, so packet timing directly affects hit registration.
   - MOHAA's pmove has no per-frame velocity snapping (unlike Q3's 125/333 fps jump physics) and chops moves into ≤ 66 ms steps (`fgame/bg_pmove.cpp:1530`), so fps doesn't change jump height (from a code read, not measured).
   - **The command rate sets movement physics** (JayRewd, 2026-10-17). pmove works out speed and direction over each command's time window, and shorter windows change step heights and sliding along surfaces: as designed up to ~85 commands/s, okay-ish at 125, noticeable at 250, a real problem at 500+ ("can't even walk on the terrain"). The server simulates the same commands, so this can't be fixed client-side. The user plays at 250 (normal mode) and walks on terrain fine. In normal mode fps = command rate, so **normal mode must stay at ≤ 250 fps** (125 / 200 / 250); high render rates only come through the decoupled mode. Above 1000 fps normal mode also runs the game clock fast (turbo); the fix comes with the command clock (82cb483d idea). *Measured in session 33 on mohdm4's terrain (§2 "Terrain and ladders in the decoupled mode"): at 500 and 1000 usercmds a second the player leaves the ground for 1–27 ms where a slope changes and against walls (0.8–1.0% of a valley walk's usercmds airborne, 5.5 landings a walk; none at 125, 1.5 at 250), and the client stutters its landing sounds, footsteps and view bob; speed changes ≤ 1.1%. Not seen: being unable to walk, on this map's walkable terrain (≤ 36°). The decoupled mode's server side is stock's at its command rate.*
   - Any limiter change must keep divisor values bit-exact (250 → every frame exactly 4 ms) and should be checked with frame-time and packet-spacing histograms.

**Planned latency work, by phase:**
- **Phase 1:** CAMetalLayer configured per rules 2–4 (drawable count, `displaySyncEnabled` from `r_swapInterval`, opaque layer, `presentsWithTransaction NO`); the wait-placement rule built into the frame loop from day one. *Done in session 2; drawables come from a helper thread with vsync off, see §3.2 "Drawable acquisition".*
- **Phase 2:** **latency probe** `cl_latencyStats 1`. For each frame, the time from the newest mouse event folded into the usercmd (mach time stamped at pump time, µs) to the frame's real present time (`MTLDrawable addPresentedHandler` → `presentedTime`). Log p50/p95/p99 over N frames, plus input→commit. For GL1, only input→`SwapBuffers` return is available (a lower bound; documented). Record SDL+Metal numbers windowed and fullscreen in §2. *Done in session 5: §2 "Input → present latency" (numbers and the Instruments cross-check), §3.2 "Added in session 5" (design). It also reports GPU-done times and the OS event timestamps.*
- **Phase 3:** direct-to-display verified in fullscreen and borderless fullscreen; Info.plist Game Mode keys; latency numbers per display mode recorded. *Done in session 6: the window shadow kept fullscreen from going direct. Both fullscreen modes now go direct on every frame: pump → present 2.1 ms at 250 fps, and Core Animation's present feedback is right. Borderless fullscreen = `r_fullscreen 1` + `r_noborder 1`. Game Mode turns on in both. See §2 "per display mode" and §3.2 "Added in session 6". Tell the user: play in fullscreen or borderless, not in a window.*
- **Phase 5 (performance and latency):**
  - targets the session 5 probe found (§2):
    - the compositor's two latency modes in a window (~5 vs ~9.7 ms at 250 fps);
    - the ~0.3 ms from commit to GPU start; *session 28: the GPU waking up from idle; woken when the frame starts (`re.WakeGPU`), commit → GPU start ~0.6 → ~0.35 ms and the frame on screen ~0.35 ms sooner at 250 fps (5f, §2)*;
    - the vsync queue (11.9 ms in fullscreen) and the late GPU finish with vsync on;
  - tune frames in flight / drawable count with the probe; *session 26: 2 drawables stay (3 queue flips and cost ~0.6 ms); frames that find no drawable are presented late by the drawable thread instead of skipped (5d, §3.2 "Added in session 26")*;
  - **raw mouse input via GCMouse** (GameController framework: unaccelerated HID deltas from a high-frequency handler, accumulated off the main thread and read at `IN_Frame`), usable while SDL still owns the window. Pulled ahead of Phase 6 because it's the biggest input-path win; verify first whether SDL's relative mode on macOS applies pointer acceleration;
  - **Client timing redesign (approved by the user 2026-10-16, both parts):**
    1. **Precise pacing, the default.** A µs-precise frame limiter on `mach_absolute_time` (sleep with `mach_wait_until`, or `kevent` EVFILT_TIMER with `NOTE_CRITICAL|NOTE_MACHTIME`, minus a learned oversleep estimate; at least one network poll per frame; a final spin of ~50–100 µs with no system calls). Caps are honored exactly in µs (JayRewd's approach). Divisor caps stay tick-exact as in stock (250 → every frame 4 ms). Non-divisor caps run at the requested rate instead of stock's round-up: **stock's integer-ms limiter (`minMsec = 1000/com_maxfps`) turns 240 into 250 fps; JayRewd's µs limiter, and ours, honor 240 exactly.** In classic mode (one command per frame) their command lengths then alternate (4/5 ms at 240), which is what any client at such a frame rate sends; in the decoupled mode commands keep their own exact clock. Vanilla is already near tick-exact for divisors, so the expected gains are less polling CPU (~1 ms/frame today), exact non-divisor caps, correct behavior above 1000 fps (with the `Com_ModifyMsec` 0 ms fix), and an fps counter in µs. JayRewd's present guard (never present two frames closer than the cap) is **not used**: it waits after input sampling (§4b rule 1) and mainly serves VRR, which the user will never use. Commands, `serverTime` and `msec` stay whole milliseconds. Measure vanilla's frame-time and packet-spacing histograms first, then compare.
       **The user's Vulkan branch did this part** (pstngh/openmohaa-vulkan `vulkan-renderer`, 413c50d1 "microsecond frame limiter for com_maxfps" and e43e3e1d "start frames on the millisecond tick at caps dividing 1000", 2026-10-17; read in session 28 at the user's request, "maybe inspire from it": ideas only, re-implemented here). What to take:
       - **A deadline that advances by exactly one period** (1000000 / cap µs, rounded up so the rate never exceeds the cap), the old `bias` gone; a frame late by less than a period is made up by the next, one later than that restarts the deadline from now (no catch-up burst). Measured there: 144 / 165 / 240 exact (were 167 / 167 / 250), frame starts 2–10 µs over the period at p99.
       - **Caps that divide 1000 keep a whole-millisecond deadline on `Sys_Milliseconds`' tick** (e43e3e1d, the important finding): a µs deadline sits anywhere in the millisecond, and `com_frameTime` is read 7–14 µs (p99 up to 47 µs) after the wait ends, so a deadline just before a tick put some reads in the next millisecond: **frames alternated 3 and 5 ms at 250 instead of 4** (every frame is a usercmd, a pmove step), 58 such frames per 5 × 60 s at 125 and 500, up to half the frames for a deadline 990 µs after the tick. With the tick kept, every frame at 125/250/500 is 1000 / cap ms again. Non-divisor caps keep the µs deadline (6 and 7 ms frames at 144 are what that cap asks). They predict the next tick from the last one seen while polling (`Sys_Milliseconds` and the µs clock at the same rate on Linux; a disagreement over 50 µs resyncs).
       - **The wait:** `select` on the network sockets (packets still read as they come) until 1 ms before the deadline, then poll; polling the last millisecond was the only variant that shortened input → present (by 0.02–0.05 ms), sleeps of 30–100 µs saved CPU (0.16 vs 0.27 of a core) but let the core clock down and lengthened it by up to 0.03 ms. On Linux the timer slack goes to 1 µs.
       - **They keep the 1 ms floor** (uncapped = at most 1000 fps; a cap ≥ 1000 = the floor alone): a frame is a usercmd with whole-millisecond game time, and a 0 ms frame becomes 1 ms in `Com_ModifyMsec` (the game clock runs ahead). So **lifting the ~1000 fps cap needs part 2's command clock**; part 1 alone can't (rule 7: above 1000 fps classic mode is turbo, and above 250 commands/s movement bends).

Every difference from the Vulkan branch and from this plan decided by measurement on this Mac (the user, session 28: "anything the vulkan port does different than our original plan, we should make sure if optimal for our metal port"), input → screen first, then CPU:
         1. **The sleep: a kqueue EVFILT_TIMER with `NOTE_CRITICAL` and no leeway** (this plan's), not `select` (the Vulkan branch's) nor `mach_wait_until`: macOS coalesces both by ~20–25% of the timeout at any thread QoS (a 2.4 ms sleep wakes 0.61 ms late; it gave the old limiter's 7/8/9 ms frames at 125), the critical timer ~25 µs late (p99 ~55) at any length. **No learned oversleep estimate:** at ~25–55 µs the polled margin covers it, and frames start within ~5 µs of the deadline (p99.9).
         2. **The polled margin: half of a focused client's frame**, neither the Vulkan branch's 1 ms nor this plan's 50–100 µs: the margin decides the cores (250 fps: 0.3 ms polled → 10% of the frames on a performance core, 1 ms → 84%, 2 ms = half → 100%; 125: 1 ms 10%, 2 ms 79%, 4 ms = half 100%), and a frame on an efficiency core takes ~1.5 ms instead of ~0.2. Frame start → on screen at 250 fps, p50: the old limiter 3.66 ms, 1 ms polled 2.74, half 1.98, a busy wait 1.82; the first frame of a flick, pump → commit: 1.80 / 0.60–0.74 / 0.25 / 0.23 ms. CPU at 250: ~43% of a core (1 ms) against ~54% (half). The user's choice, §3.1 #19. QoS: the main thread is already `USER_INTERACTIVE`; `NSActivityLatencyCritical` doesn't help.
         3. **The clock: no tick prediction, and `Sys_Milliseconds`' time base unchanged:** `Sys_Microseconds` reads the same `gettimeofday` clock in µs, so the tick is known exactly. `gettimeofday` against `mach_absolute_time`: +4.2 ppm over 30 s, +5.4 ppm over 5 minutes (1.6 ms): the Vulkan branch's prediction from the last tick would work too (µs off per frame), but needs a resync path for nothing.

Held frames (a scratch `s29hitch` command) at 250: 5 ms → 5 + 3 ms, then 4; 12, 30 and 300 ms → every following frame 4 ms. The old `bias` sent 1–3 ms catch-up commands after every long frame (30 ms → 1, 3; 300 → 2, 2; at 125: 30 → 2, 6, then 7/8/9).

Packets are capped at 125/s (`cl_maxpackets`), so 250 commands reach the server in the same packets at the same moments as 125. 250 only splits each packet into two 4 ms physics steps, which bend step heights and slides. Rendering runs at any rate (uncapped or any cap, not just divisors of 1000), and every rendered frame uses the newest mouse input for the view. Prediction-error detection/smoothing in cgame's `CG_PredictPlayerState` must ignore it. Key changes or latched taps inside a command window can cause small corrections.
       - (b) **JayRewd's lerp:** shows the state at `cg.time − interval`, i.e. 0..1 interval older than the newest prediction (~2 ms average at 250/s). The safe fallback.

The next scheduled command carries the fire button with those angles; later commands use the live angles again. Commands stay perfectly regular.

Every command the server receives is a physics step, so an extra short command bends movement; JayRewd's own test build came to the same conclusion. Extrapolated inputs fail too; anything finer than the command needs a new protocol (sub-tick timestamps), which existing servers don't have.
       Click-time aim sends no extra commands and no made-up data: the same single 125/s command, whose angle is the one the player really had at the click. It reaches the server in the same packet, so it doesn't get the shot there sooner; it fixes aim drift during flicks. Side effect: that one command's movement direction uses the click-time angle (negligible: a few degrees for one 8 ms step during a flick). View angles are already decoupled (updated every render frame, sent with each command).
       **Check:** local firing feedback (muzzle flash, recoil, view-model animation, sound) shows on the frame of the click via predict-to-now, if MOHAA's cgame predicts it locally; otherwise note what waits for the server.

Each difference from JayRewd's decided by the stream the server receives (a local server logging what it runs):
         1. **The rate:** 85–250, whole milliseconds (theirs 85–125, `cl.serverTime`'s steps). Ours runs on `com_frameTime`, so the windows are whole milliseconds of input as stock's frames; at 250 the server gets stock 250's lengths (4 ms 92.0%, 5 ms 5.3%, 2 ms 2.7%, the time delta's steps) and packets, at 125 stock 125's.
         2. **The usercmd's time:** its own frame's (`CL_SetCGameTime`'s, without the clamp to the last drawn frame), not stock's frame before: with frames at any rate the frame before is no whole interval back, and the clamp ate the −2 ms steps (125: 7 ms 2.7% where stock has 6 ms 5.3%). Stock's usercmd carries the time one frame back (4 ms at 250); ours carries its own, so the predicted player and the world meet on the usercmd's frame.
         3. **The angles:** never changed after a usercmd is made (theirs rewrite the newest every frame); cgame takes the live angles from a usercmd one past the newest, never sent (`CL_GetUserCmd(cmdNumber + 1)`), applied to the view only. Every drawn frame's view equals the live angle (100% within 0.01°).
         4. **Key taps:** stock's `CL_KeyState` over the usercmd's window (theirs count a tap as a full press). At the same pump rate identical to stock; rendering faster pumps the keys at their own millisecond, so a press inside a window gives a fraction, the down time per press kept.
         5. **Keyboard turning:** on the usercmd, by its window's game time (stock's code; theirs per render frame, clamped to 1 ms): the stream equals stock's, but `+left`/`+right` turn the view in usercmd steps. Per frame would need µs key times.
         6. **0 ms frames:** allowed at `timescale` 1 in the decoupled mode only (as theirs); the game clock stays real time (×1.000).
         7. **Not theirs:** a usercmd ahead of the render cap gets a frame of its own (no drawing); a frame due just before the usercmd's tick waits for it (packets 69.7 → 97.8% within ±125 µs uncapped, 94.9 → 99.8% at 960); divisor caps keep to the usercmds' ticks (render 250 + usercmds 250: one frame for both).
         Left for the second half: the movement shown between usercmds ((a) predict-to-now / (b) their lerp, by the probe and `cg_showmiss`), click-time aim (**the server aims with the packet's eye angles**, cgame's last drawn view, so the latch must cover them too), the 0 ms frame pass (effects, sound, `wait`, AVI), terrain, the user's online test.
       - **JayRewd's b26d8a67** (JayRewd/openmohaa-vulkan, 2026-10-18, sent by the user in session 30 before approving session 31; read from the code, not run): "A client cap above 1000, and an uncapped client, waits on the microsecond deadline instead of the 1 ms floor", for their real-time fpsbench. Their branch has no command clock at that commit (no `cl_cmdfps` in `cl_input.cpp`) and stock's `Com_ModifyMsec`, so with `com_maxfps 0` (a common setting) or above 1000 every sub-millisecond frame is bumped to 1 ms of game time and makes a usercmd: the client's clock (`cls.realtime`, `cl.serverTime`) runs as many times fast as frames per millisecond, the time delta is pulled back only at snapshots (fast adjusts and resets), and **OpenMoHAA's game drops every usercmd stamped later than its own time** (`Player::ClientThink`: `serverTime > level.svsTime` → return, the usercmd's movement and buttons lost, after `SV_ClientThink` has taken it as the last one). Rule 7's turbo, plus lost usercmds online; a local bench runs its game clock fast. **Not ours:** we lift the floor only with `cl_cmdRate`'s clock (stock mode keeps 1 ms). Worth telling JayRewd (gate it on a command clock or the bench).

A real-time bench (actual pacing, not a timedemo) reports p95/p99/p99.9 frame times and *suggests* a cap of floor(p99 fps / 100)·100 − 100. That closes the gap between p99 and p99.9 for consistent frame times. The trade-off: slightly higher average latency than uncapped; the user chooses. It also answers which render cap the Mac sustains (e.g. 480 / 720 / 960 at 1080p in a busy match). In the decoupled mode any render cap is fine; in classic mode it never suggests above 250 (physics) and only divisors of 1000 (125 / 200 / 250), since non-divisors make uneven commands. It prints the value / a ready command and never writes archived cvars itself; temporary cvars are never saved into the config, even on a crash.
    4. ***Dropped by the user in session 63 (§3.1 #37): vsync off stays the lowest latency, and plain vsync (`r_swapInterval 1`) the tear-free option. The design, kept as it was:*** **Low-latency vsync, the tear-free option** (moved up 2026-10-17: with a cap at the refresh rate and vsync off, the tear line parks in one spot). `displaySyncEnabled YES`, 2 drawables, 1 frame in flight, paced by `CAMetalDisplayLink` (`preferredFrameLatency` 1). **Just-in-time frame start:** sleep *before* input sampling so the frame finishes just before the vsync deadline (a moving estimate of frame work time + margin; §4b rule 1 stays intact). Compare with the latency probe against vsync off at the same cap. *(Session 75's paced presents, §3.1 #49 and `r_metalPacedPresent`, are another thing: the frames keep their start and rate, only the presents are paced, one per refresh.)*
    **Recommended setup for the user** (240 Hz display, no VRR, recorded 2026-10-17):
    - Decoupled mode, commands at 125/s (250 optional for the familiar feel), click-time shot aim, vsync off, fullscreen direct-to-display.
    - Render cap 960 (or 1000) if the part 3 bench shows the Mac holds it at p99 at 1080p in a busy match, otherwise 480. Multiples of 240 park tear lines in fixed spots (four tiny ones per refresh at 960); 1000 makes them roam. The user picks by eye.
    - Tear-free alternative: 240 + low-latency vsync (part 4). *(Dropped in session 63, §3.1 #37: `r_swapInterval 1` is the tear-free option.)*
    - In classic mode: stay at ≤ 250 fps (125 / 200 / 250). 500 / 1000 break movement physics (rule 7), and above 1000 is turbo. Classic mode warns above 250 and hard-caps at 1000. (Corrects session 1's earlier "500 / 1000" advice.)
    The user will never use VRR: no VRR work, no present guard.
    *Session 31's probe (§2 "The movement between usercmds and click-time aim"): rendering at 960 / 1000 / uncapped doesn't bring the view to the screen sooner in the Space yet (at most ~470–500 frames a second shown, pump → present p50 +0.4–0.5 ms against stock 250), and the mode's frames have a slow tail; until session 32 explains it, don't recommend a render cap above 250 for latency.*
    *Session 32 (§2, the input's age on screen, the Space, 1080p, a quiet scene): **render 480** shows input ~1.0 ms sooner than 250 (p50 3.6 against 4.6 ms, p95 4.8 against 6.6) with ~99% of its frames shown; 960 is no better (half its frames never show: the display takes ~500 images a second with 2 drawables), and 3 drawables don't help; **uncapped** is ~0.4 ms better still (3.16 / 4.25) because its GPU never idles, at the cost of a whole performance core and the GPU drawing ~3500 frames a second. So the recommendation becomes: `com_maxfps 480` in the mode, `0` (uncapped) for the last ~0.4 ms if the user accepts the power; the "busy match at p99" check of part 3 still applies.*

The vertex-by-vertex loop with a `switch` per light and a data-dependent branch per term, built with `-fno-strict-aliasing` (every byte store forces the light data to be reloaded), cost ~3 ns per term.
- **Change 1: `RB_Light_Real` goes light by light** (`tr_sphere_shade.cpp`, the multi-light case). The light is copied to a local, the `switch` runs once per light, and each light loops over all vertexes into a static per-vertex accumulator; the directional term is branch-free (`fDot = fDot > 0 ? fDot : 0`) and clang vectorizes it 4 vertices wide (`ld4` normals, `fmaxnm`, `fmla`, `st3`). Each vertex still adds its lights in the original order with the same expressions: **bit-identical** (A/B build: 0 of 83 MB of colors differ over the whole bench, 0 on m2l1). Session 11 result (5a continued, the user away): **skinning and sphere lighting of skeletal models on the GPU**, bit-identical to the CPU.
- **What the bench draws** (temporary counters, then reverted): ~68 skeletal surfaces in ~45 batches and ~8500 vertices per frame. 95.5% of the vertices go through the vertex-lit fast path (`RB_StageIteratorVertexLitTextureUnfogged`), and 99.6% of those are lit by `RB_Light_Real` without the cube map. 64% are on entities with morphs, 29% on meshes > 0, and 29% of the batches hold several surfaces. No dlights, and LOD collapse on 95% of the vertices. At most 72 bones per model and 820 vertices per surface. So the GPU path has to cover morphs, meshes > 0 and merged batches; the other 4.5% (multi-stage shaders, generic iterator) stay on the CPU.
- **Design** (§3.2 "GPU skinning"):
  - `mb_skin_vs` in `tr_mtl_stage.metal` computes what `RB_SkelMesh` and `RB_Light_Real` computed, then continues exactly as `mb_stage_vs`. The fragment shader, the pipelines' other state and the draw order are unchanged.
  - `RB_SkelMesh` still does the LOD and builds the indices, but leaves the vertexes to the GPU as a job of the batch.
  - The vertex-lit iterator hands the jobs and the sphere's lights to `mbSkinBegin`; positions, texcoord 0 and colors are no longer copied into the ring.
  - Whatever needs the CPU vertexes after all (a cube-map sphere, another color function, dlights, `r_showtris`/`r_shownormals`, the shadow shader, `r_primitives 1/3`, any other iterator) gets them from `RB_SkinMaterialize`, which runs the old loops (now `RB_SkelMeshVertexes`, moved verbatim).
  - Static data (copied once, `mbSkinStatic`): each surface's vertex records, verbatim, behind one word per vertex giving the offset of its record; and a bone map per (tiki, mesh > 0), replacing `TIKI_GetLocalChannel` per weight.
  - Per draw (in the ring): the jobs, the lights (`reallightinfo_t` verbatim) and the ambient. Each entity's bones (`skelBoneCache_t`) and morph weights are copied once per scene.
  - `r_metalSkinning 0` turns it off (the CPU path, for comparisons).
- **Exactness by construction:**
  - `MB_Skin` runs in safe math (`#pragma METAL fp math_mode(safe)`: the AIR has no fast-math flags and no `fmuladd`; checked in the IR).
  - Each `a*b + c` that clang fuses on the CPU (`-ffp-contract=on`: one fma per C expression, the left product of `a*b + c*d`, compound `+=` included, checked in clang's IR) is an explicit `fma()` in the same order.
  - The divisions are `precise::divide`.
  - The colors get arm64's float → int conversion (toward zero, NaN → 0, saturating) and the int clamp with wrapping addition.
  - The single-light, multi-light and no-light cases keep their different alpha and rounding.
- **Verified with an A/B build** (`port/skinab.sh`, kept as a tool; the patch is `port/skinab_patch.py`, never applied to the tree). Every GPU-skinned batch is drawn the GPU way and then the CPU way. Both vertex shaders capture their outputs per vertex, and after each frame the backend compares them bit for bit: clip position, color, texcoords, eye z, clip distance. It also compares the GPU's skinned positions, lit colors and unquantized light sums with the CPU's.
  - Whole bench: 99,506 batches, 19.6 M vertices (19.1 M captured, 19.07 M GPU-lit, 18.0 M light sums). **0 differences in every field.**
  - Same on dm6fx (2.07 M vertices), m2l1 (single-player, 0.98 M), obj3 (0.63 M, mostly single-light), Spearhead `shot_sh` (1.1 M) and Breakthrough `shot_bt` (1.25 M). dm4 and dm5 show no skeletal model.
  - The harness does see differences: a dot product associated the other way gave 31 colors off by one level in 19 M (a mistake that rounds only once is that rare after quantization, which is why the light sums are compared too).
- **Bench**, same sitting, **screen locked** the whole time:
  | Build | ms work per frame |
  |---|---|
  | metalref (aa3dc22e) | 0.288 / 0.289 / 0.290, again 0.294 / 0.290 / 0.290 |
  | metal (GPU skinning) | **0.231 / 0.228 / 0.226**, again 0.228 / 0.229 / 0.230 |
  | metal with `r_metalSkinning 0` (the CPU path) | 0.293 / 0.292 / 0.291 (metalref right after: 0.290 / 0.290) |
  | GL1 | 0.778 / 0.780 / 0.772 |
  - **−0.061 ms per frame (−21%).**
  - An unlocked single run earlier in the session gave 0.234 (the lock state then wasn't checked).
  - GPU (`port/bench.sh trace`, same sitting): 0.087 ms per game frame vs metalref's 0.083, at 8.7% utilization. The skinning costs the GPU ~4 µs per frame.
  - The first run with a new build creates the skin pipelines (max frame 28 ms once); the pipeline cache covers them from then on.
- **Fixed views** (`port/shot.sh regress base-s9`, with GPU skinning on): identical to the Metal baseline except the views that vary from run to run (dm6 view 8's weapon bar, 1998 px; dm5's snow; dm6fx views 4–7, firing; m2l1 view 0, 11 px). dm6fx view 2, the soldier close-up, is identical. Against GL1, the same numbers as sessions 9–10: dm6 1454 / 135 / 496 / 2533 / 1404 / 152 / 117 / 1 / 2437, dm6fx 0 / 4 / 605, m2l1 4253 / 753, dm4 843 / 1694 / 323 / 521, obj3 11389 / 16 / 14151.
- **Where the frame goes now** (`sample` of the looped timedemo, ~13,700 frames; `sample` inflates the frame to ~0.28 ms), ms per frame:
  | Where | ms/frame |
  |---|---|
  | backend `RB_ExecuteRenderCommands` | 0.092 |

  | of it: `RB_SkelMesh` (LOD + indices only now) | 0.011 |

Where the remaining ~0.23 ms goes (session 13's last profile, `s13all2`: 3140 frame-work samples over ~13,500 frames ≈ 0.232 ms per frame, the bench's figure):
- **Metal and the driver, ~17%** (+3% ring copies): AGX, IOGPU/IOKit, the kernel and objc under the backend. That is the per-draw state emission in `drawIndexedPrimitives` (~58 draws per frame) and the fixed per-frame costs (`MB_BeginPass`: command buffer and scene encoder; `mbEndFrame`: commit, the final pass, present, the frame-slot wait; together ~7%). Fewer draws means merging batches, which changes the draw order (not bit-identical). The fixed costs come with the frame structure.
- **Engine-side, ~42%:** cgame's own work (~18%), the UI widgets, the client frame, the SDL pump and OpenAL (~19%), and the skeletor's animation called from the front end (`TIKI_GetFrameInternal`, ~5%). None of it is renderer code.
- **Renderer CPU, ~38%:** the front end without the skeletor (~17%: world walk, entity surfaces, sort) and the backend's own code (~21%: the surface functions, the iterators, `MB_PrepareDraw`). What was cheap to cut exactly has been cut; omaha's exact world culls are the next candidates (above).

Each trigger costs 250–400 µs on the main thread: `S_OPENAL_StartSound` → `openal_channel_two_d_stream::set_sfx` → `S_CodecGetSound` tries the WAV, MP3, OGG and Opus codecs in turn, each `FS_FOpenFileRead` misses in the two directory search paths, and each miss runs `FS_CorrectCase` (`access` + `opendir`/`readdir` of the parent), then the warning is printed. Nothing remembers the failure. Both volumes are case-insensitive APFS, so `FS_CorrectCase`'s directory scan can never find anything there. 20 of the 23 frames above one run's p99 had ≥ 150 µs in cgame's `S_StartSound`; server-sent sounds hit the same path from the demo parse (`demo` 266–521 µs at frames 296, 864, 2252). Engine-side (client sound code and `qcommon/files.cpp`), not renderer: the follow-up is in §6.

No pipeline was created and no image uploaded during the timedemo (first-use costs are all at load). The other p99.9 frames (e.g. 1087–1093 in one run, 4.4 / 2.3 / 2.2 ms) are not repeatable: scheduling noise.
  - In MOHAA the 2D draws flush the pending render commands (`Draw_StretchPic` → `R_IssuePendingRenderCommands`), so the 3D backend runs inside cgame's draw, and `RE_EndFrame` only presents (~5–15 µs).

A per-face cull would save their sort and backend work but costs a sphere test on all 478; the estimate is ≤ ~2 µs net per frame, under what the bench resolves, and the whole BSP walk is 14 µs. omaha's flat leaf list / 8-leaf group culls bound the gain at a few µs more. Not done; the sound fix above is worth ~100× more at p99.

Session 14, continued: **5c, the engine-side p99 tail** (the user moved it ahead of Phase 7, §3.1 #8). Both changes are outside the renderer and keep the output the same:
- **Confirmed:** the dialogue lines are missing from the retail data. `sound/dialogue/Generic/A/damage/` in Pak4 holds only `dpl_damage_13i.wav`, and there are no `death` files at all; the aliases reference more variants than the game ships, so the original game fails on them too. Streamed sounds are never checked at registration (`S_LoadSound` returns at once for them), so every start opened the file.
- **Change 1** (9e1c543f, `snd_openal_new.cpp`, `snd_dma_new.cpp`, `snd_local_new.h`): `openal_channel_two_d_stream::set_sfx` marks the sfx `SFX_FLAG_STREAM_FAILED` when `S_CodecLoad` fails, and returns at once on later starts (with the same side effects: `stop()`, the channel fields). `S_BeginRegistration` clears the flag on every sfx, so each map load (after any download) searches again. cgame calls `S_RegisterSound` on every trigger, so the flag can't be reset there. Warnings per run: 83 → 29 (once per missing file per map).
- **Change 2** (0d0b3148, `qcommon/files.cpp` `check_filecase`): every file read from a pk3 first misses in the two directory search paths, and each miss ran `FS_CorrectCase`: `access()` on every path component, then an `opendir`/`readdir` scan of the first missing component's parent. On a case-insensitive volume `access()` already ignores case, so the scan can't find anything: `check_filecase` now asks that directory's own volume (`pathconf(dir, _PC_CASE_SENSITIVE)`) and skips the scan when it says 0. Exact across mount points; case-sensitive volumes still scan. It also speeds up every streamed sound that does exist (each start opens its file).

Session 27 result (5e, the pipeline items; the user away at the start (8 min idle), back once mid-session and asked before the bench: "Run them now" for the runs that take the cursor, "Not now" for the parts that need them; commits on `metal`, not pushed: Phase 5 isn't done):
- **The pipeline cache was mostly broken, and silently.** `serializeToURL:` fails ("Failed to generate machO … expecting 'fragment' stage in pipeline no. N") on an archive that was read from a file and then got pipelines added, for some sets of pipelines: reproduced outside the game (`build.noindex/s27/archtest`): an archive of `final` + `0x0e001` read back, plus `0x0e089` or `0x0e005`, fails; plus `0x0e003` or `0x2e001` works; a dozen additions failed every time; with or without the depth query pipeline. After a failed serialize, the same archive object writes only what was added after the failure (session 19's "1 pipeline instead of 13"). This client routes the renderer's `PRINT_WARNING` to `Com_DPrintf` (developer only), so nobody saw it: every bench run in session 26's logs found 2 of its 15 listed pipelines in the archive and compiled the other 13 at startup (cheap only because the system shader cache had them). `metalref` shows it plainly: a menu-only run, then the bench twice: "pipeline cache not written" on both (with `developer 1`), the archive stuck at the menu's pipelines, 10 created at their first draw on every run.
- **A fresh archive always serializes** (archtest: 5, 24 and 45 pipelines, the query among them, every one found after reading it back). So the cache now writes a new archive holding every pipeline the process created (their descriptors are kept), never the one it read; only when the run compiled a pipeline (`mb_archiveDirty`), ~30 ms at the quit or `vid_restart`. A failed write leaves the old archive and prints a visible line; the keys file is written whenever the list grew, even then (a listed key the archive lacks is compiled up front by the next run, never in play). `MB_CACHE_VERSION` 2, now part of the file names' hash, retires version 1's archives. **The query pipeline stays in the archive:** a fresh archive with it reads back fine, and the failure came with or without it.
- **Pipelines ahead of their first draw** (`R_PrecacheShaderPipelines` in `FinishShader`, `R_PrecacheState` next to `R_State`, `mbPrecachePipeline` / `mbPrecacheFinish` in the backend): each shader, when it is loaded, describes the state each of its stages draws with, as the stage iterators set it up: the generic iterator per stage (blend, alpha test, one or two texture units), the vertex-lit fast path also with GPU skinning, the lightmapped multitexture path, the sky's outer box; plus ProjectDlightTexture's two passes (models under dynamic lights) at startup. The backend takes a missing pipeline from the archive at once, else compiles it with `newRenderPipelineStateWithDescriptor:completionHandler:` on Metal's threads (up to 64 at a time). A draw that needs one still compiling waits for that one only; `RE_EndRegistration` (the end of `CL_InitCGame`) waits for the rest, so none is compiled in play. The startup's keys list goes the same way (its misses compile in parallel). `R_State` is unchanged: a first version moved its blend switch into a helper, which stayed an out-of-line call per blend change, so the factors became a table in `R_PrecacheState`.
- **Measured:**
  - archtest, variants the system shader cache had never seen: 5–30 ms each one at a time on the calling thread; 8 at once with the async call: submitted in ~2 ms, all done 37 ms later on Metal's threads. A process's first pipeline call costs ~10 ms (the compiler service's connection), the first specialization of `mb_stage_fs` ~10 ms.
  - Empty cache, the bench demo (dm6): 16 of 17 pipelines compiled ahead of their first draw (the slowest done 0.6 ms after its submission; 0.0 ms waited at the end of the load). The one created at its first draw is `0xe548`, the console's untextured box (`DrawBox`; the console and menu only, never predicted; the keys list has it after one run). Before (`metalref`): all 14 at their first draw.
  - Warm: 17 of 17 listed pipelines from the archive at startup in 1.2 ms (before: 2 of 15, the rest compiled), none compiled ahead or at a first draw, nothing written. A menu-only archive (6) + the bench map (11 new): written, the next run 17 of 17 from the archive. dm/mohdm4 after dm6: 1 new variant compiled ahead (0.4 ms, nothing waited), written, the next run 18 of 18; m2l1 and obj/obj_team3 after that brought nothing new.
  - The bench's keys: `0e001 0e003 0e005 0e007 0e089 0e119 0e11b 0e149 0e14b 0e189 0e309 0e459 0e548 0e549 0e54b 2e001 2e005` (`0e11b` and `0e14b`, two multitextured blends, are predicted but not drawn there).
- **Bench, ABBA ×4** (`build.noindex/s27/ab.sh`, each flavor with its own pipeline cache: `metal` and `metalref` delete each other's files; `metalref` = ff5691e2, the session's start; unlocked, nobody on the input, load 2.5–4.2): `metal` 0.217 / 0.215 / 0.218 / 0.216 / 0.217 / 0.218 / 0.217 / 0.217 ms work (mean 0.2169), pooled p50/p95/p99/p99.9 207/359/470/667 µs; `metalref` 0.214 / 0.221 / 0.214 / 0.218 / 0.217 / 0.217 / 0.215 / 0.217 (mean 0.2166), 207/362/479/623 µs. **Equal.** (The first version, with the helper in `R_State`, 3 rounds earlier: 0.2188 vs 0.2168 over 12 runs each, within the noise; the helper went anyway.)
- **Checks:** build (the install signs and checks the seal); `port/glcheck.sh` clean; renderer warnings none new. Rendering can't change (the same descriptors, created earlier), so no fixed views.
- **Tools** (scratch, `build.noindex/s27/`): `archtest.m` (the archive outside the game: `open <file|new>`, `get <key>`, `query`, `final`, `save <file>` (version 1's write), `fresh <file>` (a new archive of everything created), `async <keys> end`), `ab.sh` (ABBA bench, one pipeline cache per flavor in `cache/<flavor>/`, numbering continued from the files in `ab/`).

Session 28 result (5f, the GPU's wake-up before each frame; the user at the machine at the start, asked: "Run them now" for the runs that take the cursor, "Not now" for their parts; then away, the screen locked ~20 min after their last input, asked again: "Unlocked, run them"; commits on `metal`, not pushed: Phase 5 isn't done):
- **What the ~0.37 ms from commit to GPU start is: the GPU powering up after idling.** Outside the game (`build.noindex/s28/gpustart`: no window; per period one command buffer, a 1920×1080 render pass with ~0.16 ms of GPU work, committed 0.25 ms after the "frame start", 2 in flight; paced exactly by sleeping to 1.5 ms before the start and spinning, because a sleeping thread woke up to ~0.8 ms late): commit → GPU start p50 **0.12 ms at a 1 ms period, 0.33 ms at 2 ms, 0.57 ms at 4 ms, 0.58 at 8 ms** (p95 0.17 / 0.40 / 0.70 / 0.72); the minimum ~0.06–0.1 ms at every period. After ~1.3–1.5 ms without work the GPU goes to sleep, and the next commit waits ~0.3–0.5 ms for it. The bench never shows it (~1000 fps: 0.124 ms in `r_metalPresentStats`); at 250 fps every frame paid it (in play, the Space: 0.60–0.64 ms mean).
- **A tiny command buffer ahead of the frame wakes it.** gpustart at 4 ms, the frame's GPU end in µs after its start (committed at ~260): no kick ~935–1019; a blit committed at the frame's start ~750; 0.3 ms before it ~680; 0.8 ms ~640; 1.0 ms ~612; 1.3 ms ~590; 1.6 ms ~780; 2 ms ~878 (the GPU has gone back to sleep). The kick's own commit → start is ~0.5 ms (it pays the wake-up instead of the frame). Blit, compute and render kicks do the same; an empty command buffer never reaches the GPU ("done" in 0.3 µs) and wakes nothing. A kick costs 16–33 µs of CPU (p50), a process's first one 0.4–1.2 ms (the driver's first blit or command setup).
- **In the game** (`re.WakeGPU`, §3.2 "Added in session 28"): the renderer commits a 4-byte blit fill when the engine starts a frame, unless something was committed within the last millisecond. Placement, measured with temporary counters (`build.noindex/s28/dbg.patch`, never committed; GPU start after commit by the kick's lead before the frame's commit, the Space at 250 fps): lead 0.2–0.3 ms → 0.35 ms; 0.4–0.8 ms → 0.23–0.28; 0.9–1.6 ms → 0.29–0.38; 1.7–2.0 ms → 0.37–0.55 (dozing again); no kick 0.66. A first version kicked inside the frame limiter's wait, in its last millisecond: only 46% of the frames got one (the limiter's 3 ms `select` often wakes past the frame's tick, and its last-millisecond branch never runs), and the ones that did came 1.4–1.9 ms ahead of the commit. A kick right after the wait, before `IN_Frame`, lands 0.5–0.6 ms ahead (the frame's pump → commit) on every frame: the best spot, and one call site.
- **Measured** (`build.noindex/s28/run.sh`: `MOUSE=0 LATSTATS=2` runs of `port/latency.sh`, dm/mohdm6, `com_maxfps 250`, vsync off, 15 s; `fr.py` pools every frame's commit, GPU-done and present times from `cl_latencyStats 2`; `r_metalWakeGPU` 0/1 alternating, the same binary; unlocked, nobody on the input, load 2.1–4.7). µs, p50 / p95 / p99, 4 runs each pooled (19 k frames) in the Space, 2 each in exclusive:

  | Mode | `r_metalWakeGPU` | commit → GPU start (mean) | commit → GPU done | commit → on screen |

Session 29 result (§4b part 1, the µs frame limiter; the user at the machine at the start, asked: "Run them now" for the runs that take the cursor; away ~45 min during the runs, back for the decision: §3.1 #19, and "Yes, run them" for the synthetic mouse; commits on `metal`, not pushed: Phase 5 isn't done):
- **The wait, measured outside the game** (`build.noindex/s29/waittest.m`: a frame loop of busy work, a sleep to a margin before the deadline, a spin to it; this M4's CPUs 0–5 are efficiency cores, 6–9 performance, `ioreg` `cluster-type`):
  - `select` and `mach_wait_until` wake late by ~20–25% of their timeout, at the default QoS and at `USER_INTERACTIVE` alike (timer coalescing): a 0.6 / 1.6 / 2.6 / 3.6 ms sleep 0.13 / 0.33 / 0.53 / 0.73 ms late; a 25–50 ms `select` 3.5–5 ms. `NSActivityLatencyCritical` changes nothing. `kevent` with a timeout: ~13%.
  - A kqueue EVFILT_TIMER with `NOTE_CRITICAL | NOTE_LEEWAY` 0: ~25 µs late at p50, ~52–58 at p99, ~100–300 at p99.9, at any length (0.3 to 50 ms). Re-adding the oneshot timer clears a firing that happened while nobody waited (`kqstale.c`).
  - `gettimeofday` (`Sys_Milliseconds`' clock) runs 4.2 ppm faster than `mach_absolute_time` (NTP): ~0.02 µs per 4 ms frame.
- **The cores, the session's main finding.** With the new limiter polling the last millisecond (the Vulkan branch's wait), the game's main thread (already `QOS_CLASS_USER_INTERACTIVE`: an app's main thread) ran 84% of its frames on a performance core at 250 fps and 10% at 125; the old limiter 14% and 7%. **On an efficiency core the frame's work takes ~1.4–1.9 ms, on a performance core ~0.16–0.2 ms** (and ~0.4 ms on a performance core at a lower clock). macOS puts a thread that sleeps more than it works on the efficiency cores. The share follows the polled part of the frame (250 fps: 0.3 ms 10%, 1 ms 84%, 2 ms 100%; 125: 1 ms 10%, 2 ms 79%, 4 ms 100%; the whole frame (`com_busyWait 1`) 100%), so the wait polls half of a focused client's frame (100% at 125, 144, 240, 250 and 500 in every run; ~52–55% of a core). Game Mode was on (the Space) in every run; `NSActivityLatencyCritical` didn't help (69% at 250, 11% at 125). The game's process CPU: 250 fps 58% → 59%, 125: 34% → 54%, 500: 57% → 68%, uncapped unchanged (110%).

Session 34 result (the alpha-test depth prepass test; the user at the machine at the start (HIDIdleTime 9 s): the online test "Later, not now", "Run them now" for the runs that take the cursor; then away; no code change, only the docs; commits on `metal`, not pushed: Phase 5 isn't done):
- **Measured first** (§2 "The alpha-tested draws' GPU time, the depth prepass and the draw order"): the Space at 1920×1080 in the decoupled mode, at 960 and uncapped, on mohdm5, obj_team1, obj_team2, mohdm4 and m2l1. The GPU limits uncapped on mohdm5 and the obj maps (busy 95–99%), and on mohdm5 already makes the CPU wait now and then at 960 (GPU 0.74–0.88 ms a frame). The alpha-tested draws (static tree and bush models, treeline and hedgerow cards) are up to 75% of the GPU's time on those views (mohdm5 ~75%).
- **The prepass prototype: dropped.** Per alpha-tested batch, depth only then shaded with depth EQUAL: mohdm5 +11–15% GPU time at 960 and −4 to −11% frames/s uncapped, obj_team2 worse too, only obj_team1 uncapped gains (+0–11%). MOHAA's foliage is one texture times the vertex color, so the depth pass costs what the shading did.
- **Found instead: draw the alpha-tested surfaces after the opaque ones.** A stable partition of the opaque range after the sort: mohdm5 −8 to −26% GPU time at 960, uncapped up to +20% frames/s; neutral (±4% at 960, ±2% uncapped) on obj_team1, mohdm4 and m2l1; obj_team2 uncapped +0 to +7%, at 960 one view +14% where the GPU is 35% busy. The image differs only in tie pixels (≤ 90 of 921,600, max 17). Front to back within a shader adds −1.5 to −4% on mohdm5. At 480 / 250 the GPU's clock governor blurs it (one run: mixed at 480, −6 to −31% at 250). Implementing it is session 35's slice.
- **Every timing segment's frames on a performance core** (≥ 99.8%) but one (84.4%, obj_team2 uncapped). No bench: no code changed (`s34x` is HEAD plus the scratch instrumentation).

Plan (session 1):
- Latency work from §4b (frames-in-flight tuning, GCMouse raw input, the client timing redesign: precise pacing by default + the optional decoupled command/render mode + the percentile cap suggestion + low-latency vsync, activity/QoS/Game Mode, audio latency), measured with the latency probe.
- Measure first (bench + `trace` + `sample`/Time Profiler), one change at a time, each recorded here with before/after numbers. Candidates:
  - Static world geometry in GPU-resident buffers (no per-frame re-tessellation/copy).
  - Batching by shader+lightmap; sort keys to minimize PSO/state changes; fewer render passes.
  - GPU skinning (compute) for TIKI; GPU tcMod/tcGen/rgbGen/deforms for the common cases.
  - Faster `RB_Light_Real` sphere lighting.
  - BC texture compression for memory; async texture loading at map load.
  - Metal 4 (argument tables, residency sets, `MTL4CommandQueue`) where measured.
  - Frame pacing (present timing / CAMetalDisplayLink).
- Engine frame floor: `Com_Frame` pads frames to 1 ms with an integer-ms clock, which caps fps near 1000. Making it µs-precise changes how `com_maxfps` behaves online (frame pacing feeds usercmd timing and movement feel), so **ask the user before touching it**.
- **Done when:** the bench work time is ≤ 0.25 ms/frame or the remaining cost is documented as engine-side, p99 frame time is lower than GL1, input→present latency is measured lower than the Phase 2 numbers (and as low as the display mode allows), and the fixed views (`port/shot.sh pair`) show no visual change (since §3.1 #20: no change that isn't deliberate and recorded).
  - *Status after session 14:* work time **met** (0.234 ms, the rest documented above); fixed views **met** (every change, `regress base-s9`); **p99 vs GL1 met** (session 14: work p99 739 µs vs GL1 2318, p99.9 1536 vs 3490, pooled over 8 runs each, unlocked; after 5c ~500 µs, 4.7× below GL1); **latency open** (after Phase 6, on the native input layer, §3.1 #8; `port/latency.sh` takes the mouse: with the user). *Session 26:* exclusive fullscreen and the borderless window no longer lose frames while another application draws on the other display (5d, late presents); the probe check against the Phase 2 numbers with the synthetic mouse still needs the user. *Session 28:* the GPU is woken when a frame starts (5f): commit → on screen ~0.35 ms shorter at 250 fps (Space 2.36 → 2.00 ms p50). *Session 43:* all four met, **Phase 5 done** (the last group, §3.1 #21: MOHAA's dlights made cheaper exactly). *Session 39:* **latency met** (§2 "The Phase 5 latency check"): pump → present in a window 10.02 / 12.16 / 12.35 → 1.98 / 4.45 / 4.64 ms, exclusive 1.88 / 3.86 / 3.99, the Space 1.83 / 1.98 / 2.14; input on screen soonest in the Space at 480 with the decoupled mode (3.55 ms p50).

- Then native `NSWindow` + `CAMetalLayer` view, keyboard (NSEvent → Q3 keys, text input), raw mouse (GCMouse deltas, cursor capture; moved here from the Phase 5 latency list), ~~gamepad (GCController)~~ (dropped by the user, §3.1 #12), clipboard, window modes, Retina, ~~the `openmohaa://` URL handler~~ (removed instead, the user, §3.1 #13), the color cursor.
